name: ha--bedrooms-night-fixed-cooling-contract
description: The contract the user states for the small bedroom at night: fix the temperature, disengage the program, let the air conditioner hold it by itself. This eval asserts that contract structurally and behaviourally. Structurally, the proportional comfort-band branches must carry the suppression guard 'not (summer_night_window and is_state(...night_fixed_cooling, on) and not away)', and the fixed branch must read its setpoint from the input_number rather than a literal. Behaviourally - which is the half that can actually be wrong without anyone noticing - the AC setpoint must be written once at the 19:30 handover and never again until morning, measured from history over the last four nights.

changes: C5 computes setpoint changes on the UNFILTERED history series and only then labels them as inside or outside the night window. Filtering first makes every window boundary look like a write, which is how an earlier ad-hoc version of this measurement produced four phantom writes all stamped 19:30.
C6 asserts the handover lands on the helper's current value, so the contract stays asserted against the setting rather than against a number frozen into the check.

logic_model.js loads both sources of truth once: the repository (main.tf, import.tf, helpers.json) and the live instance (/api/config/automation/config, /api/states, /api/services, /api/template, /api/history).

main.tf mixes two serialisations of the same field - 102 fields are HCL-escaped JSON on one physical line, 177 are multi-line jsonencode([...]) expressions. A parser that handled only the first found 25 Jinja templates; handling both finds 248. Every comfort band, i.e. all of the actual control logic, uses the second form, so the naive parser reported empty on exactly the automations worth checking.

jsonencode bodies are not parsed by hand. They are written out as terraform outputs and evaluated by terraform itself, because terraform is the authority on its own syntax and a hand-rolled HCL subset parser is one more thing that can be quietly wrong. The result is cached under a key derived from main.tf's own bytes, so the cache cannot go stale.

Comparison is done on a canonical form: HA emits trigger/action objects with either the modern (trigger:, action:) or legacy (platform:, service:) key spelling and pluralises the top-level keys, so both sides are normalised before diffing to stop a core upgrade reading as 98 automations of drift.

validation.result: 6/6 checks passed against the live instance. suppression guard present on 3 proportional branches (expected >= 3) fixed branch reads night_fixed_cooling_target rather than a literal both entry triggers defined (19:30 clock + toggle turning on) helpers live: toggle=on, target=24.0 setpoint writes inside the night window excluding the 19:30 handover: 0 19:30 handovers observed: 2, landing on a value other than 24: 0
checks: C1: the suppression guard is present on all three proportional branches
C2: the fixed branch reads night_fixed_cooling_target, not a hardcoded number
C3: both entry triggers exist (the 19:30 clock trigger and the toggle turning on mid-window)
C5: LIVE, 4 nights - zero setpoint writes inside the night window other than the 19:30 handover
C6: LIVE - every observed handover lands on the helper's value
measured: C1 PASS: suppression guard present on 3 proportional branches (expected >= 3)
C2 PASS: fixed branch reads night_fixed_cooling_target rather than a literal
C3 PASS: both entry triggers defined (19:30 clock + toggle turning on)
C4 PASS: helpers live: toggle=on, target=24.0
C5 PASS: setpoint writes inside the night window excluding the 19:30 handover: 0
C6 PASS: 19:30 handovers observed: 2, landing on a value other than 24: 0

incidents.what: The first behavioural measurement reported zero automation fires for the entire night window, which would have meant the whole loop was dead.
incidents.detected_by: The number was too clean. Zero fires across four nights is not a plausible reading for a running system.
incidents.fix: Removed minimal_response from the history queries.
incidents.root_cause: minimal_response strips attributes from the history response, and last_triggered is an attribute. The query was asking for exactly the field it had told the API to omit.

incidents.what: The first measurement reported four setpoint writes inside the night window, all stamped 19:30 - i.e. it appeared to contradict the contract.
incidents.detected_by: All four were at the same clock time on four different nights, which is the signature of a window artefact rather than of a control fault.
incidents.fix: Setpoint changes are computed on the unfiltered series and only labelled by window afterwards.
incidents.root_cause: Filtering the series to the window first makes the first sample inside the window look like a change from nothing. Every window boundary becomes a false positive.

notes: Passes. The contract holds. What this eval deliberately does NOT assert is that the room reaches the fixed target: measured over four nights the AC's own sensor sits a median 1.0 C BELOW its own setpoint while still calling for cool, and the room lands a median 0.9 C low, bottoming at 22.8 C against a 24.0 C target. That is the unit's own thermostat undershooting, not the program failing to disengage, and it is a separate question from the one this eval answers.
